entities.summary:
Henry White was a prominent American diplomat who played a crucial role in shaping the Treaty of Versailles, one of the most significant diplomatic agreements of the 20th century. Born into a family of modest means, White's early life was marked by his exceptional educational achievements, which ultimately led him to attend Harvard University and later the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy.

White's diplomatic career spanned over three decades, during which he served as a key advisor to several U.S. presidents, including Woodrow Wilson and Warren G. Harding. His most notable achievement was his role in negotiating the Treaty of Versailles, which officially ended World War I and imposed harsh penalties on Germany.

However, White's legacy is also marked by controversy, particularly surrounding his involvement in the Red Scare of the 1920s. As a vocal critic of communism, he played a key role in the persecution of suspected radicals and was even involved in the infamous Palmer Raids.

Despite these controversies, White remains an important figure in American diplomatic history, and his contributions to the field continue to be studied by scholars today.
